Altimeter's Brad Gerstner Says Nvidia Was Priced for "Negative Growth for 2028 and 2029." Wall Street Expects 29% ©@jiefeng jiang from Getty Images via Canva, @metamorworks from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) jumped 31.5% on Monday after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, but it still traded at about 11x forward earnings at the close.

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner says that multiple priced in shrinking growth for 2028 and 2029, while analysts expect revenue and earnings to keep climbing.

The main risk is that hyperscalers have stopped raising their capex forecasts, which matters for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) too.

The stock depends on its 2028 estimates holding, and the hyperscalers' reports in late January and early February are the next test.

NVIDIA jumped 31.5% on Monday, Nov. 23, after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after he resigned.

But Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner thinks the bigger story is how cheap the stock got before the jump.

On Monday's Halftime Report, Gerstner said that as of that morning, "what was imputed into the NVIDIA multiple was actually negative growth for 2028 and 2029. I think it's nuts."

Wall Street expects the opposite.

And NVIDIA isn't the only one with a lot riding on 2028. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) and AMD need those years to hold too.

Wall Street still sees growth in both years

On CNBC's Power Lunch, Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said the Street expects NVIDIA's revenue to grow 72% in calendar 2027 and 29% in calendar 2028.

TIKR's consensus has revenue more than doubling, from $424 billion in the year ending January 2027 to $927 billion in the year ending January 2029:

Nvidia (NVDA): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to January) (TIKR)

Earnings follow the same path. Analysts expect normalized EPS to climb 31%, from $16.61 in the year ending January 2028 to $21.77 the year after:

Nvidia (NVDA): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to January) (TIKR)
The market is priced for a peak

Now look at what investors pay for that growth. Even after Monday's jump, NVIDIA traded at about 11x forward earnings at the close. That's up from a five-year low of 8.7x on Friday, but far below its five-year average of 35x and its peak of nearly 70x in May 2023:

NVIDIA (NVDA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

A multiple that low only makes sense if investors expect those 2028 estimates to be cut hard, as if this cycle peaks in 2027.

TIKR tracks 61 analysts on Nvidia. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia's Analyst Ratings

Capex forecasts have stopped rising

The worry is NVIDIA's customers. As Wedbush's Matt Bryson put it on CNBC's Closing Bell, "it feels like the entire AI trade is assuming that there's deterioration either in 27 or 28."

title: 'Big Short' Investor Michael Burry Just Closed His Bet Against the Nasdaq. Here's What Investors Should Do Now
detail:
'Big Short' Investor Michael Burry Just Closed His Bet Against the Nasdaq. Here's What Investors Should Do Now
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 5:20 PM CST 4 min read
NVDA
^IXIC
PLTR
MET
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Michael Burry made his name betting against the housing market before the 2008 financial crisis. This week, with tech stocks in a steep slide, he did something somewhat unusual for him: He stopped betting against the market.

In a post on his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, Burry said he had sold the rest of his put options on the Nasdaq-100, bearish bets that pay off when the index falls. "Globally, my portfolio is more long, and less short, than it has been in some time," he wrote. Apart from puts on Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and MetLife (NYSE:MET), he added, "I am temporarily almost entirely long."

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Why the Timing Matters

Burry is turning more bullish after a sharp drop. The Nasdaq Composite closed Tuesday at 23,733.54, down 14.5% from its Oct. 6 close, and the Nasdaq-100 fell 16% over the same stretch. The Composite is down about 7% in November alone, as doubts about whether the AI spending boom will pay off, new tariff proposals, and the turmoil around Nvidia's leadership have weighed on AI stocks.

Puts gain value as an index falls, so selling them after a slide is a way to lock in profits. Burry said much of his cash, about 25% of the portfolio, came from profitable put options plus money added to the account.

He Isn't Calling a Bottom

The most important word in his post may be "temporarily." Burry said he is "continuing to assess short opportunities," and he hasn't said the market has bottomed. He also kept his Palantir puts, even though Palantir shares, at about $164 on Wednesday, already sit roughly 23% below their 52-week high.

Burry disclosed large put positions on Nvidia and Palantir in late 2025 after warning about an AI bubble. Shifting from that stance to mostly long tells you he thinks a good part of the downside he expected has now played out, at least for the broad index.

What Investors Should Do Now

For most investors, the answer is not to copy his trades. Burry can reverse a position in a day and write about it afterward, so by the time a move becomes news, he may have changed it again. Short-selling and options are tools most individual investors shouldn't rely on.

The useful lesson is in how he's behaving. He took profits on a bet that worked, he's holding a big cash cushion, and he's staying selective about what he owns. You can do a version of that: Make a list of quality tech stocks you'd be glad to own for five years, and buy them in stages if the sell-off continues, rather than all at once. Keep enough cash on the side that you're never forced to sell in a downturn.

title: The Nvidia Scandal Set Off a Chip Crackdown in Congress. Which Stocks Are Most at Risk?
detail:
The Nvidia Scandal Set Off a Chip Crackdown in Congress. Which Stocks Are Most at Risk?
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 5:18 PM CST 5 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has spent November at the center of a political storm, with Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO amid allegations that its chips were smuggled into China. The stock fell another 4% on Wednesday. But the company most at risk from Washington's response may be one most investors don't connect to the scandal at all.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Congress Is Getting Tougher

In a note published Wednesday, research firm TS Lombard said the Nvidia fallout has galvanized lawmakers, putting Congress on track to pass three to four new chip export-control measures, most likely as part of the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act. Grace Fan, the firm's managing director of global policy and disruptive themes research, said passage is a question of "when" and not "if," though a government shutdown fight around the Dec. 11 funding deadline could push it into early 2027.

The bills would close several loopholes at once. One would give Congress a say over exports of the most advanced AI chips. Another would require location tracking on exported AI chips to stop smuggling. A third would target Chinese companies renting U.S. chips through overseas cloud services. The centerpiece, the MATCH Act, goes after the machines that make chips rather than the chips themselves.

Why ASML Is in the Crosshairs

The MATCH Act would pressure U.S. allies, mainly the Netherlands and Japan, to match U.S. restrictions on the sale of chipmaking equipment to China. If they don't, TS Lombard said, the Senate version would direct the Commerce Department to impose the controls itself after about 150 days. The Senate bill also names every deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machine among the tools that couldn't go to China at all.

That's why TS Lombard says the companies most at risk aren't U.S. equipment makers such as Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT), Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX), and KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC), which already face U.S. rules. Instead, it points to ASML (NASDAQ:ASML), the Dutch lithography leader, and Japan's Tokyo Electron, along with several other Japanese suppliers. The Dutch government has said it opposes the bill.

Wednesday's trading didn't reflect that ranking. Lam fell 6% and Applied Materials 4%, while ASML dropped 2.5% to about $1,303, roughly 35% below its 52-week high.

title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
detail:
S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang gestures as he speaks during the World Economic Forum (WEF) annual meeting in Davos on January 21, 2026. The World Economic Forum takes place in Davos from January 19 to January 23, 2026. (Photo by Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP via Getty Images) | Image Credits:Fabrice COFFRINI/AFP / Getty Images
Marina Temkin
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 4:44 PM CST 1 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia's rating, citing concerns about the company's management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia's strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about "weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning" and "key man risk," meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.

The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia's rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang's ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.

A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

Trading disclosure

Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) has agreed to pay $290 million to settle an investor lawsuit.

The 2018 suit alleged the company misled shareholders about the portion of its GPU sales attributable to cryptocurrency mining.

Related: Nvidia's earnings call names two former crypto miners

Nvidia clubbed crypto mining-tied GPU sales under gaming segment, suit alleged

The lawsuit, filed December 2018, accused Nvidia and its founder Jensen Huang of misleading shareholders about its gaming revenue during 2017-18.

During the crypto boom of those years, miners turned to Nvidia chips to mine cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin (BTC). 

The investors accused the company of allegedly understating over $1 billion in GPU sales tied to crypto mining. They claimed the company sold a large number of its GPUs to miners but clubbed the revenue under the gaming segment.

Investors looking at the gaming segment's strong growth interpreted it as evidence of sustainable demand from gamers. But when crypto prices crashed in 2018, mining demand collapsed and Nvidia was left with excess GPU inventory and weaker sales.

The company's earnings call and guidance cut on Aug. 16 and a revenue warning on Nov. 15 the same year disclosed this crypto mining exposure, with shares dropping on both occasions, the suit alleged.

Nvidia settles lawsuit for $290 million

Nvidia has decided to settle the investor lawsuit for $290 million, Reuters reported on Nov. 25.

A company spokesperson said, "NVIDIA resolved a class action litigation regarding the state of the PC gaming market nearly a decade ago. NVIDIA appreciates the contributions of its insurers in helping wrap up this legacy matter and funding the majority of the $290 million settlement. The settlement remains subject to court approval."

That annual dividend currently stands at $2.12 per share, or $0.53 each quarter.

So, to earn a healthy $1,300 per quarter in dividends, how many shares would you need to own? Well, it's as simple as dividing $1,300 by 0.53.

You would need to own 2,453 shares to generate that much quarterly dividend income. That's a hefty investment: That many shares would cost $240,394 at the current share price of $98.

And second, while the rise of GLP-1 drugs is hurting some snack food and beverage companies, about 68% of Coca-Cola's portfolio consists of low- or no-calorie drink options.

So, you might not be able to afford enough KO shares to generate over $1,000 in income per quarter, but an investment in this stock is, in my opinion, a wise one.
